plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.6.7
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a spherical wedge in 3D, the volume element used for triple integration in spherical coordinates. The wedge is a small solid (shown with orange, yellow, and green faces) bounded by six surfaces: two spherical shells at radii rho1 and rho2 (marked along the z-axis), two vertical half-planes at azimuthal angles theta1 and theta2 (shown in the horizontal plane near the base), and two cones at polar angles phi1 and phi2 (measured from the z-axis and indicated by arcs). The bounding surfaces are rendered transparently to reveal the wedge's position inside the overall spherical sector. The figure defines the spherical wedge as the three-dimensional analogue of the polar rectangle and identifies its six bounding surfaces in terms of the spherical coordinates rho, theta, and phi.

elements: Coordinate axes (x, y, z) extending from the origin, with arrows and labels at their tips
Solid spherical wedge (volume element) with 6 distinct faces
Transparent grey spherical sector providing context, bounding the volume from origin to rho2, between theta1 and theta2, and from z-axis to the xy-plane
Arc for theta1 in the xy-plane from the x-axis to the theta1 half-plane
Arc for theta2 in the xy-plane from the x-axis to the theta2 half-plane
Arc for phi1 in the theta2 half-plane from the z-axis down to the phi1 cone
Arc for phi2 in the theta2 half-plane from the z-axis down to the phi2 cone
Dimension lines parallel to the z-axis (offset to the left) indicating lengths rho1 and rho2, with accompanying labels
Labels for theta1, theta2, phi1, phi2 near their respective arcs

interactions.teaches: Inspect the 3D shape of the spherical wedge and its bounding surfaces from any angle

interactions.teaches: Moves the inner spherical boundary, changing the wedge's distance from the origin

interactions.label: ρ₂ (Outer Radius)
interactions.teaches: Moves the outer spherical boundary, expanding the radial thickness of the wedge

interactions.teaches: Rotates the starting vertical bounding plane around the z-axis

interactions.label: θ₂ (End Azimuth)
interactions.teaches: Rotates the ending vertical bounding plane, expanding the wedge horizontally

interactions.label: φ₁ (Top Polar Angle)
interactions.teaches: Adjusts the upper conical boundary, tilting the top of the wedge downward from the z-axis

interactions.label: φ₂ (Bottom Polar Angle)
interactions.teaches: Adjusts the lower conical boundary, dropping the bottom of the wedge toward the xy-plane

demo_steps.title: The Spherical Wedge
demo_steps.narration: A volume element in spherical coordinates is bounded by two radii, two azimuthal angles, and two polar angles.

demo_steps.title: Radial Bounds (ρ)
demo_steps.narration: Increasing ρ₁ and ρ₂ moves the wedge outward along the radial direction. The transparent shell grows to match ρ₂.

demo_steps.title: Azimuthal Bounds (θ)
demo_steps.narration: Changing θ swept angles rotates the wedge around the z-axis, sliding it along the xy-plane.

demo_steps.title: Polar Bounds (φ)
demo_steps.narration: Adjusting φ angles moves the wedge vertically. Notice how the top and bottom faces are curved sections of cones.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Coordinates: x = rho*sin(phi)*cos(theta), y = rho*sin(phi)*sin(theta), z = rho*cos(phi). Scale: axes extend to 6 units. Wedge colors: outer face (rho2) green #8fb38f, inner face (rho1) yellow #e3cc73, side faces (theta1, theta2) orange #e5a855, top/bottom faces (phi1, phi2 cones) red #d66b5d. The transparent shell bounds the region: rho in [0, rho2], theta in [theta1, theta2], phi in [0, pi/2]; color it grey #cccccc with 0.15 opacity. The rho dimension lines should be drawn vertically at a fixed offset of x = -1.5, y = -1.5 (or screen-left), spanning from z=0 to z=rho1 and z=rho2. The theta arcs lie flat on z=0. The phi arcs should be drawn in the vertical plane defined by theta2. Rebuild the custom parametric geometries for the wedge faces whenever sliders move.
interactionPlan.notes: Use ParametricGeometry (or construct plane/sphere/cone segments via vertex manipulation) to perfectly form the 6 non-planar faces of the wedge. Ensure the bounds in the sliders are converted to radians for trig functions. Keep the axes fixed; only rebuild the wedge, transparent shell, arcs, and dimension lines reactively.

authoredContext:
By a spherical wedge or spherical element
of volume we mean a solid enclosed between six surfaces of the following form:
two spheres (green) ρ = ρ1,ρ = ρ2 (ρ1 <ρ2)
two vertical half-planes (yellow) θ = θ1,θ = θ2 (θ1 <θ2)
nappes of two circular cones (pink) φ = φ1,φ = φ2 (φ1 <φ2)
(Figure 14.6.7). We will refer to the numbers ρ2 − ρ1,θ2 − θ1, and φ2 − φ1 as the dimensions of a spherical wedge.

discrepancies: The transparent reference shell only spans between the wedge's azimuthal angles (θ₁ to θ₂), whereas the source figure's shell spans a full 90-degree octant from the x-axis to the y-axis.
The θ₁ and θ₂ angle arcs have double-headed arrows in the generated figure, but single-headed arrows pointing outward in the source.
The horizontal lines connecting the z-axis to the ρ dimension lines are dashed in the generated figure, whereas they are solid in the source figure.
The text labels (especially for the Greek letters) appear noticeably smaller relative to the figure size than those in the source.
evaluation.notes: Excellent interactive figure with accurate projection, mapping, and colors; the only notable flaw is the truncated azimuthal span of the background transparent shell.
action_items: Change the transparent shell's azimuthal bounds (`uDim`) to span from `0` to `Math.PI/2` so it forms a full octant instead of being cut off at θ₁ and θ₂.
Modify the arc drawing logic so that the azimuthal (θ) arcs only have a single arrowhead at their ending point.
Change the horizontal reference lines for the ρ dimensions from dashed to solid.
Increase the `fontSize` in `labelOpts` (e.g., to '36px') so the angle and radius labels are more prominent.

feedback.rationale: High scores across the board with no failure modes indicate the figure is already excellent; the noted discrepancies are minor stylistic details that do not warrant further iteration.
